subject: Peter
note: Evidence for the first enhanced Bible figure page. Every quotation is in peter.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/peter/ (gitignored). The Bible is the Berean Standard Bible (public domain); the chapters quoted are copied into bsb-peter-chapters.txt.

life.text: Simon's home town was Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Philip.
life.source: John 1:44 (BSB): "Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter." Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1: "from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee".
life.note: No source gives a birth year.

life.text: He shared a house at Capernaum with Andrew; Jesus healed his mother-in-law there.
His father was John (John 1:42; 21:15) or Jonah (Matthew 16:17); his brother was Andrew.
He was married: Paul says Cephas took along a believing wife. Clement of Alexandria says Peter had children, and tells of his wife's death.
life.source: 1 Corinthians 9:5 (BSB); Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 3 and 7, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 30 (McGiffert, NPNF2 1): "For Peter and Philip begat children"; "when the blessed Peter saw his own wife led out to die, he rejoiced ... Oh thou, remember the Lord."
life.note: The wife's death is marked on the page as "A story Clement heard" (Clement: "They say").

life.text: He was a fisherman in partnership with James and John, the sons of Zebedee.
life.source: Luke 5:10 (BSB): "and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee".

life.text: Cephas is Aramaic for rock; Peter (Petros) is its Greek translation.
life.source: John 1:42 (BSB): "You will be called Cephas" (which is translated as Peter). Britannica, "Saint Peter the Apostle": "He received from Jesus the name Cephas (from Aramaic Kepa ['Rock']; hence Peter, from Petros, a Greek translation of Kepa)." Catholic Encyclopedia: "in Aramaic in which the same word (Kipha) is used for 'Peter' and 'rock'".

life.text: He is named first in every list of the Twelve; Matthew calls him "first".
life.source: Matthew 10:2; Mark 3:16; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13 (BSB). Britannica: "Whenever the disciples are listed, Peter is invariably mentioned first."

life.text: The Greek word for a charcoal fire (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament: John 18:18 and John 21:9.
life.source: Bible Hub, Strong's Greek 439 (biblehub-strongs-439.txt): "Strong's Greek 439 2 Occurrences", John 18:18 and John 21:9. The whole BSB has "charcoal fire" only in these two verses.
life.note: Corrected 2026-09-26: the page first said "The Bible". Thayer (same page) lists the word also in Sirach 11:32 and 4 Maccabees 9:20, which are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, so the claim holds only for the New Testament.

life.text: The risen Lord appeared to Simon; Paul's list of witnesses begins with Cephas.
About three thousand were baptized at Pentecost; the number of men grew to about five thousand after the second sermon.
life.note: Only the 3,000 is on the page.

life.text: 153 large fish, and the net was not torn.
Mark's Gospel is Peter's preaching written down, says Papias; Irenaeus says the same.
life.source: Papias, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 39; Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 1 (ANF 1).

life.text: 1 Peter was accepted; Eusebius had learned that 2 Peter was not in the canon, though many used it; Jerome says many doubted it for its style.
life.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 3; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1.
life.note: The page says "the second letter under his name" wherever it quotes 2 Peter.

life.source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note to 1 Clement: "the Epistle may be dated about a.d. 97".

life.text: A fishhook (agkistron) appears once in the New Testament, Matthew 17:27, where Jesus tells Peter to cast a hook for the temple tax.
life.source: Bible Hub, Strong's Greek 44 (biblehub-strongs-44.txt): "The term appears a single time in the Greek New Testament"; "Strong's Greek 44 1 Occurrence". BSB Matthew 17:24-27 ("the two-drachma tax"); Britannica calls them "the collectors of the temple tax". A search of the BSB New Testament for "hook" finds only Matthew 17:27 (the other hits are "shook").
life.note: Added 2026-09-26 as the fifth "Did you know?" tidbit.

death.text: He died at Rome under Nero. Tertullian: "Then is Peter girt by another, when he is made fast to the cross" (the ANF note cites John 21:18). Lactantius: Nero "crucified Peter, and slew Paul".
death.source: Tertullian, Scorpiace, chapter 15 (ANF 3), footnote 8327 "John xxi. 18"; Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 2.

death.text: The year is not settled: Jerome gives Nero's fourteenth and last year; Eusebius's Chronicle 67 or 68; Harnack and Duchesne 64; Britannica says 64.
death.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. Peter": "The date of Peter's death is thus not yet decided"; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25; Britannica.

death.text: Origen says he was crucified head-downwards at his own request, giving no reason; the Acts of Peter (by 200) has it with a mystical reason; Jerome (392) gives the reason of humility.
death.source: Origen, Commentary on Genesis, volume 3, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 1; Acts of Peter, chapters 37 and 38 (M. R. James, 1924; his introduction: "not later than A. D. 200"); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1, written "the fourteenth of the Emperor Theodosius" (chapter 135), that is 392.
death.note: NPNF's footnote to Jerome's preface prints "a.d. 492", a misprint for 392.

death.text: Gaius, about 200, could show the "trophies" of the apostles on the Vatican and the Ostian way; the word is understood of the tomb. Constantine built a basilica over Peter's grave, replaced by today's St Peter's.
death.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25, with McGiffert's note 543 (Caius "at the beginning of the third century held a disputation with Proclus in Rome"); Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. Peter" (burial place).
death.note: The excavations under St Peter's (1940s to 1960s) are left off the page: no checked public-domain source was fetched.

death.text: Jerome: Peter was "Buried at Rome in the Vatican near the triumphal way". Eusebius introduces Gaius as speaking "concerning the places where the sacred corpses of the aforesaid apostles are laid"; Gaius himself says only "I can show the trophies of the apostles", at the Vatican or the Ostian way, without saying whose is where.
death.source: npnf203.txt (Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1); npnf201.txt (Church History, Book 2, chapter 25, sections 6 and 7).

rome_and_primacy.text: Witnesses to Peter at Rome: 1 Peter 5:13 ("Babylon", read as Rome by Papias and Clement according to Eusebius 2.15); Ignatius, Romans 4; Dionysius of Corinth (Eusebius 2.25); Irenaeus 3.1 and 3.3; Gaius (Eusebius 2.25); Tertullian, Prescription 36.
rome_and_primacy.source: Fetched texts: bsb-peter-chapters.txt, anf01.txt, anf03.txt, npnf201.txt.
rome_and_primacy.note: McGiffert (a Protestant scholar) calls the joint founding of the Roman church by Peter and Paul "a very early fiction" (note 552), since there were believers at Rome before either came; the page says only what Irenaeus says.

rome_and_primacy.text: Irenaeus: the apostles committed the episcopate to Linus; Eusebius counts Linus first; Jerome gives Peter twenty-five years in the chair at Rome. Britannica: the Catholic Church recognizes him as the first of its popes.
rome_and_primacy.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 2; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 1; Britannica.

rome_and_primacy.text: The Catholic reading of Matthew 16:18: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870), chapters 1 and 2, in Schaff's English.
rome_and_primacy.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, volume 2 (archive.org creedsofchristen0002phil, OCR), page 259: chapter 1 quoted word for word (read in the scan); chapter 2 paraphrased ("lives, presides, and judges, to this day and always, in his successors the Bishops of the Holy See of Rome").

rome_and_primacy.text: The Orthodox reading: Chrysostom, Homily 54 on Matthew, "that is, on the faith of his confession"; the OCA's reading for 29 June is a sermon of Augustine saying the Church is built on Peter's confession; the Longer Catechism of Philaret (approved by the Holy Synod) names Christ the only Head (question 259) and an ecumenical council as the authority over the whole Church (question 278).
rome_and_primacy.source: New Advent, Homily 54 on Matthew (NPNF1 10; CCEL's copy runs Homilies 52 to 54 together under one heading); OCA, 29 June; Schaff, Creeds of Christendom 2 (CCEL creeds2.vi.iii.ii), tr. R. W. Blackmore.
rome_and_primacy.note: The OCA's sermon is paraphrased, not quoted: its English is the OCA's own and not public domain. Schaff's heading gives the catechism as printed at Moscow, 1830; the page gives no year.

rome_and_primacy.text: Augustine held both readings and left the choice to the reader.
rome_and_primacy.source: Augustine, Retractationes, Book 1, chapter 21 (Latin, augustinus.it): "Harum autem duarum sententiarum quae sit probabilior, eligat lector." Written of a book from his time as a presbyter ("eodem presbyterii mei tempore scripsi"); he cites Ambrose's hymn on the cock-crow ("cantatur ore multorum in versibus beatissimi Ambrosii").
rome_and_primacy.note: Our translation, marked on the page. No public-domain English of the Retractations was found.

rome_and_primacy.text: Eusebius calls Linus "Peter's successor in the episcopate of the church there" (Church History 3.4), as well as counting Linus first after the martyrdom of Paul and Peter (3.2).
Some later Protestant scholars read the rock as Peter himself; the Lutheran Oscar Cullmann did, while holding that Peter was not the founder of any line of successors.
rome_and_primacy.source: Wikipedia, Saint Peter (wikipedia-saint-peter.txt), Protestant views: Cullmann "disagrees with Luther and the Protestant reformers who held that by 'rock' Christ did not mean Peter"; "Cullmann concludes that while Peter was the original head of the apostles, Peter was not the founder of any visible church succession" (citing Cullmann, Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, 1953).
rome_and_primacy.note: Secondary source: Cullmann's book (in copyright) was not fetched. The page paraphrases and does not quote him.

rome_and_primacy.text: Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus chapter 1, grounds the primacy on Matthew 16:17-19 (the keys) and John 21:15-17 ("Pasce agnos meos: Pasce oves meas").
rome_and_primacy.source: schaff-creeds-vol2-1905-djvu.txt, page 259 and following (the Latin column, read in the scan).

myths.text: "Quo vadis" is from the Acts of Peter, chapter 35 (James 1924), told again by Ambrose (Sermon against Auxentius, 13); in the Bible, Peter asks "Lord, where are You going?" at the Last Supper (John 13:36), which the Vulgate renders "Domine, quo vadis?".
Keys at the gates: Britannica says he is shown at the gates of heaven because of the keys (Matthew 16:19). Revelation 21:12, 21: twelve gates of pearl with twelve angels at the gates.
Mark: the rooster crows twice (14:30, 72); the other Gospels mention one crowing (Matthew 26:74; Luke 22:60; John 18:27).

art_and_names.text: The oldest image (a bronze medallion of the late 100s or early 200s) gives him a strong, roundish head and thick curly hair and beard; keys became his attribute from the end of the sixth century.
art_and_names.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), "St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles", Representations of St. Peter.

art_and_names.text: Patron of fishermen, Rome and popes; locksmiths for the keys.
art_and_names.source: Britannica: "He is the patron saint of popes and of Rome ... fishermen ... locksmiths."

art_and_names.note: Merriam-Webster has no entry for Cephas (404); Collins refused the fetch (403).

art_and_names.text: The Orthodox call Peter and Paul the koryphaioi, leaders of the apostles; the word named the leaders of the chorus in Greek tragedy. The OCA calls them the foremost of the apostles.
art_and_names.source: OCA, "The Holy Glorious and All-Praised Leader of the Apostles, Peter".

feasts.text: Catholic: 29 June, Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul; 18 November, Dedication of the Basilicas (optional memorial, in brackets); 22 February, Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter.
feasts.source: USCCB Liturgical Calendar 2026 ("29 Mon SAINTS PETER AND PAUL, APOSTLES ... Solemnity"; "18 Wed ... [The Dedication of the Basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, Apostles]"); USCCB readings page for 22 February 2025, title "Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, Apostle"; Calendarium Romanum 1969.
feasts.note: 22 February 2026 is the First Sunday of Lent, so the 2026 calendar does not print the Chair.

feasts.text: The Depositio Martyrum (354) has Peter and Paul on 29 June and dates the solemnity from 258; it has the Chair ("Natale Petri de cathedra") on 22 February.
feasts.source: Calendarium Romanum (1969), notes on 22 February and 29 June; Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. Peter", Feasts of St. Peter.

feasts.text: 1916 Roman Martyrology: 18 January Chair at Rome; 22 February Chair at Antioch; 29 June Peter and Paul; 1 August dedication of St Peter in Chains; 18 November dedication of the basilicas.
1960 reform (the calendar of the 1962 Missal): 18 January merged into 22 February; 1 August St Peter in Chains removed as a duplicate of 29 June; 22 February becomes "The Chair of St. Peter".
feasts.source: Wikipedia, General Roman Calendar of 1960; Calendarium Romanum 1969, note on 1 August (the Maccabees were only a commemoration in the feast of St Peter's Chains "usque ad annum 1960").
feasts.note: Wikipedia is secondary; the 1969 note confirms 1 August. No primary text of the 1960 decree was fetched.

feasts.text: Church of England: 29 June Peter and Paul, Apostles, a Festival; Peter may be kept alone. 18 to 25 January is the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (no Confession of Peter).

Episcopal Church: 18 January The Confession of Saint Peter the Apostle; 29 June The Apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul. Since 1908 the eight days between the Confession of Peter and the Conversion of Paul are the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.
Lutheran: LCMS 18 January The Confession of St Peter, 29 June St Peter and St Paul; ELCA 18 January Confession of Peter, 29 June Peter and Paul.
feasts.source: lsb-calendar.txt (Lutheran Service Book commemorations); elca-churchyear.txt (Evangelical Lutheran Worship, final draft 2006).

feasts.text: OCA: 16 January Veneration of the Precious Chains; 29 June Peter and Paul; 30 June Synaxis of the Twelve Apostles.
Greek: 29 June Peter (Ὁ Ἅγιος Πέτρος ὁ Ἀπόστολος); 16 January the chains (Ἡ προσκύνησις τῆς Τιμίας ἁλύσεως).
Russian Church (old calendar): Peter and Paul on 12 July civil (Минея. 29 июня); the chains on 29 January civil (Минея. 16 января).
Coptic: 5 Abib, the martyrdom of Saints Peter and Paul. Abib (Epip) runs 8 July to 6 August, so 5 Abib is 12 July.

pictures.text: Band: The Tears of Saint Peter, El Greco, 1580 to 1589, Bowes Museum B.M.642. Commons licence tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}. 3164 x 3900 on Commons; cropped to 92% of the width and 86% of the height, saved at 1562 x 1800, 304 KB. posM 50% 14%, posD 50% 18% (checked on a 390 x 335 cover crop and a 625 x 450 panel).
pictures.source: Commons file page wikitext; Wikidata Q9394999 (inception 1585, earliest 1580, latest 1589, from Art UK).
pictures.note: Other El Greco versions checked: Museo del Greco, Toledo (4099 x 5121); Nasjonalmuseet, Oslo (3116 x 4000); San Diego Museum of Art (4250 x 4892). All public domain. The Bowes version has the largest face. Licence tag re-read on the Commons file page 2026-09-26: {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}.

pictures.text: Portrait: Saint Peter, encaustic icon, St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai; 6th or 7th century (the Commons Artwork box says 7th century, the Crop file says early 6th). Licence tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}. 7792 x 13200, stored upside down with EXIF orientation 3; turned, cropped to 16.5% to 87% of the height, saved at 1256 x 1500, 415 KB.
pictures.note: The card keeps /img/personality/faces/peter.jpg, a 220 px crop of the same icon. Licence tag re-read on the Commons file page 2026-09-26: {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}.

could_not_verify: The excavations under St Peter's and Paul VI's 1968 statement on the bones: not fetched, left off.
A Merriam-Webster or Collins pronunciation of Cephas (only Wiktionary answered).
The Anglican Church of Canada's and other Anglican provinces' 18 January Confession of Peter: not checked, so not named.
A primary text of the 1960 Roman calendar (Wikipedia and the 1969 Calendarium's notes were used).
The OCA's June 29 sermon of Augustine is in the OCA's own English: paraphrased, not quoted.
Oscar Cullmann's own words (Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, 1953): not fetched; the page relies on Wikipedia's summary and quotes nothing of his.

checker_2026_09_26.method: Every claim on site/src/data/figures/peter.json read against the BSB (bsb-berean-standard-bible.txt), the fetched Fathers (ANF 1 and 3, NPNF2 1, 3 and 10, New Advent), the Catholic Encyclopedia, Britannica, the calendars and the Commons file pages. verify-quotes.mjs exits 0; saints-test.mjs passes; sheet measured at 1360 on the dev server (facts 1456, numbers 1382).
fixes: Tidbit, charcoal fire: "The Bible mentions a charcoal fire only twice" was true only of the Protestant canon in English. The Greek word (anthrakia) is also in Sirach 11:32 and 4 Maccabees 9:20 (Thayer, via Strong's 439), so it was false for Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Now "The New Testament mentions a charcoal fire only twice", cited to Strong's Greek 439 (2 occurrences: John 18:18, 21:9).

New tidbit (the numbers column was 225px short): the only fishhook in the New Testament, Matthew 17:24-27 (Strong's Greek 44, one occurrence), ending "Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours."
Also called: "The Prince of the Apostles, in older Catholic writing" implied the title is obsolete; now "in Catholic writing" (Catholic Encyclopedia title; 1916 Martyrology).

Buried (facts): "Gaius could show visitors his tomb" went beyond Gaius, who says "trophies of the apostles" at the Vatican or the Ostian way; the grave is Eusebius's reading. Now Jerome for the Vatican burial, and Gaius pointing visitors to the apostles' memorials.

Wrote: "The first was never doubted" in our voice is untrue of modern scholarship. Now Eusebius counts it undisputed; added that Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles all have both, and that some scholars today doubt he wrote them (Britannica: "though some scholars dispute this").
Feast 29 June: the comma-stacked list with "which may keep Peter alone" split into two sentences.
Feast 1 August: "Dropped in 1960" read as dropped from the 1916 Martyrology just named; now "Dropped from Rome's calendar in 1960".
Denials moment: "Twice more he was asked" is wrong for Luke 22:58-59 (one man says it, another insists); now "Twice more someone said it".
Race to the tomb: "Peter went straight in" embellished John 20:6 ("arrived just after him. He entered the tomb"); now "came just after him and went in".
Spelling in our voice: baptized to baptised (twice), paralyzed to paralysed, matching the saint pages and the page's own "Baptised" chip. BSB quotations keep their spelling.
2 Peter 3:8: "To those who scoffed" was wrong: the verse is addressed to "Beloved" and answers the scoffers. Now "From the second letter under his name. It answers those who scoffed".
Myth, upside down: the comma-stacked sentence on the Acts of Peter split.

Myth, Rome: "After that, the early writers place his death there" was unclear, and Ignatius (the next witness) does not place his death. Rewritten. "Gaius of Rome could point to Peter's tomb" overreached (Gaius names the Vatican and the Ostian way, not whose trophy is where); now "the apostles' memorials on the Vatican Hill and the Ostian Way".

Myth, first pope (fairness): "The early lists differ ... Eusebius also counts Linus first" set Eusebius beside Irenaeus against Jerome, but Eusebius 3.4 also calls Linus "Peter's successor in the episcopate". Now: the early writers count Rome's bishops from the apostles, in different ways; Irenaeus, Eusebius (with that phrase) and Jerome each in their own words; then the Catholic count.
The rock, Catholic (fairness): added the Council's own grounds, the keys and "Feed My sheep" (Pastor Aeternus chapter 1 cites Matthew 16 and John 21); the appositive split.

The rock, Orthodox: the comma-stacked catechism sentence split; reordered so the Chrysostom blockquote follows "John Chrysostom read the rock this way:" (before, it followed the catechism's answer and read as the catechism's words).

The rock, Protestant (fairness): the panel gave only the Reformation reading. Added that some later Protestant scholars, like the Lutheran Oscar Cullmann, read the rock as Peter himself while holding that Peter began no line of successors (Wikipedia, Saint Peter). Calvin's blockquote now has its own lead-in.

How he died: "He was buried on the Vatican Hill" stood flat before Gaius's "trophies". Now Gaius, Eusebius's reading of the trophies as graves, and Jerome's "buried at Rome in the Vatican near the triumphal way".

Is he a saint (fairness): "do not accept that Christ made his place pass to the bishops of Rome" now names what they do not accept: the Catholic teaching that his primacy over the whole Church lives on in the bishops of Rome.
Read next, Mark: "Mark wrote down what Peter remembered" misread Papias, whose "he remembered" is Mark; now "Mark was Peter's interpreter. He wrote down what he remembered".
Read next, Acts 1 to 12: "the Council" suggested the Jerusalem council, which is Acts 15; now "the lame man at the gate".

Miracles feature: "4 wonders in Acts" undercounted (Ananias and Sapphira and the open prison are in the list below it, and Acts 12's angel is a moment). The four are the healing stories (Acts 3; 5:12-16; 9:32-35; 9:36-42); now "healing stories in Acts".
Scope of the BSB claim (coordinator's two notes): words.note and the BSB source line no longer claim every Bible line on the page, since the quiz's own section quotes the World English Bible.
Comma stacks split: Tabitha's introduction; the Week of Prayer sentence.

Sources: Eusebius Book 3 now chapters 1 to 4; added Wikipedia, Saint Peter (for Cullmann) and Bible Hub, Strong's Greek 439 and 44. Evidence added to peter.quotes.json for three new quotations; the two Strong's pages saved to sources/people/peter/.
checked_and_held: Every BSB quotation and retelling in the moments, miracles and words (Luke 5, 22, 24; Matthew 10, 14, 16, 17, 26; Mark 9, 14; John 1, 6, 13, 18, 20, 21; Acts 1 to 5, 9, 10, 12, 15; Galatians 2; 1 Corinthians 9, 15; 1 and 2 Peter; Revelation 21), apart from the fixes above.
Numbers: 3 denials (Luke 22), 3 questions (John 21:15-17), 153 large fish and the net not torn (John 21:11), about 3,000 (Acts 2:41).

Fathers: 1 Clement 5; Ignatius, Romans 4; Irenaeus 3.1 and 3.3; Origen in Eusebius 3.1; Clement of Alexandria in Eusebius 3.30; Papias in Eusebius 3.39; Dionysius and Gaius in Eusebius 2.25; Tertullian, Scorpiace 15; Lactantius, Deaths of the Persecutors 2; Jerome, Lives 1 (twenty-five years, Nero's fourteenth and last year, the humble reason, the style of 2 Peter); Ambrose, Sermon against Auxentius 13; Acts of Peter 35, 37, 38 (James: not later than 200); Chrysostom, Homily 54; Calvin 4.6.5-6; Philaret's catechism questions 259 and 278; Augustine, Retractationes 1.21 (Latin); the OCA's Augustine sermon and koryphaioi.

Calendars: USCCB 2026 (29 June solemnity; 18 November optional memorial in brackets), USCCB 22 February 2025 (Feast of the Chair), Calendarium Romanum 1969 (Depositio Martyrum of 354: 29 June, origin placed in 258; 22 February "Natale Petri de cathedra"), 1916 Martyrology (18 January Chair at Rome, 22 February Chair at Antioch, 1 August Esquiline, 29 June text), Church of England (Festival; Peter may be kept alone), Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (18 January, 29 June, the Week of Prayer since 1908), LSB and ELW calendars, OCA 16 January and 29 and 30 June, synaxarion.gr, azbyka.ru, the Coptic synaxarium for 5 Abib.
Pictures: both Commons pages carry {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}; the alt texts match the images.
still_open: The numbers column is 74px short of the facts at 1360 (facts 1456, numbers 1382). The fairness fixes to Wrote and Buried added 67px to the facts; the new tidbit adds 205px. That is less than one item, so nothing more was added.
"First in every list of the Twelve" is said three times near the top: in the answer, on the Apostle step of his path, and in the second tidbit. The owner's call which to vary.
Cullmann is cited through Wikipedia, not his own book.
The band's alt text does not mention the small figure hurrying from the tomb at the lower left of El Greco's painting.
